questions.stem: A patient with suspected red eye has a potential emergency feature. What is the best immediate approach?
options: Stabilize the patient while confirming the diagnosis
Wait for outpatient review before any intervention
Ignore vital signs if the history is suggestive
Perform only elective testing
Treat a minor alternative diagnosis first
questions.conciseExplanation: Emergency variants require airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure thinking before definitive specialty steps. Diagnostic confirmation should not delay stabilization.
questions.highYieldTakeaway: When unstable, stabilization comes before perfect diagnostic certainty.

questions.stem: A patient presents with findings typical of glaucoma. Which next step is most appropriate in the SSM-style management pathway?
options: Confirm the key diagnosis and start first-line management
Delay care until every rare cause is excluded
Use an unrelated screening test as initial therapy
Treat only symptoms without risk stratification
Schedule routine follow-up without addressing red flags
questions.conciseExplanation: The vignette points to glaucoma, where SSM questions usually reward early recognition plus first-line management. Red flags and severity should be assessed before choosing invasive or delayed strategies.
questions.highYieldTakeaway: Recognize glaucoma and choose the safest evidence-based first step.

questions.stem: In a previous-exam-style question on retinal disease, which feature most strongly supports the diagnosis?
options: A coherent cluster of typical clinical and laboratory findings
A single nonspecific symptom in isolation
Normal objective testing despite severe claimed disease
A finding explained better by another organ system
Absence of the defining diagnostic criterion
questions.conciseExplanation: SSM stems often include one discriminating clue rather than long workups. The best answer is the option that matches the defining clinical pattern of retinal disease.
questions.highYieldTakeaway: Anchor on the discriminating clue, not on isolated nonspecific symptoms.

questions.stem: A candidate is asked about complications of cataract. Which complication should be actively prevented or monitored?
options: The common high-impact complication linked to the disease mechanism
A complication unrelated to the affected system
A benign incidental laboratory variant
An adverse event that occurs only after a different diagnosis
A normal physiologic adaptation
questions.conciseExplanation: Complication questions test mechanism and clinical surveillance. For cataract, prevention and monitoring focus on the complication most likely to change prognosis.
questions.highYieldTakeaway: Tie complications to pathophysiology and prognosis.

questions.stem: Which treatment principle is most appropriate for a stable patient with neuro-ophthalmology?
options: Use guideline-directed first-line therapy and reassess response
Start maximal rescue therapy before confirming severity
Avoid all therapy until irreversible damage develops
Choose therapy based only on patient age
Prefer obsolete therapy despite safer alternatives
questions.conciseExplanation: Stable cases usually require standard first-line therapy, monitoring, and escalation only when indicated. SSM answers penalize both undertreatment and unnecessary aggressive rescue therapy.
questions.highYieldTakeaway: Stable disease: first-line therapy, monitor, then escalate.
